[Lecture Map]{.slide-title}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Unit:** Unit V - Emerging Technologies
- **Course Outcome:** CO5 - Illustrate the emerging trends and technologies in the field of Information Technology
- **Bloom's Levels:** K1 - Remember; K2 - Understand
- **Duration:** 50 minutes
- **Central Question:** How can thousands of ordinary computers in different places work together like one giant supercomputer?
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Learning Objectives"}

[Learning Objectives]{.slide-title}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
By the end of this lecture, students will be able to:

- define grid computing and explain why it is needed;
- describe the main features of a computing grid;
- explain the architecture and working of a grid;
- compare grid computing with cluster and cloud computing;
- state the limitations and challenges of grid computing;
- identify major application areas of grid computing.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Think About It"}

[Think About It]{.slide-title}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- A single laptop would need **years** to analyse the data from a large physics experiment. How can the job finish in days?
- Millions of home computers sit **idle** at night. Could their spare power be put to use?
- An electricity grid delivers power from many plants to any socket. Could **computing power** be delivered the same way?
- Would you trust a stranger's computer to process your data?
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Why Grid Computing?"}

[Why Do We Need Grid Computing?]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- Scientific and engineering problems such as climate modelling, genome analysis, and particle physics need **huge computing power and storage**.
- Buying one **supercomputer** is extremely costly and still has a fixed limit.
- Most organisations have computers that are **under-utilised**: idle at night, weekends, and holidays.
- Resources such as data, software, and instruments are **spread across institutions and countries**.
- Grid computing links these separate resources so that they can be **shared and used together**.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="What Is Grid Computing?"}

[What Is Grid Computing?]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
**Grid computing** is a distributed computing model in which **geographically dispersed, heterogeneous computers and resources** are connected through a network and coordinated to work together on a **common large task**.

- Each member of the grid is called a **node**.
- To the user, the grid appears as **one virtual supercomputer**.
- Nodes may belong to **different organisations**, each keeping control of its own resources.
- Resources shared include **processing power, storage, data, software, and instruments**.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Power Grid Analogy"}

[The Electric Power Grid Analogy]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
| Electric Power Grid | Computing Grid |
|---|---|
| Many power stations feed one network | Many computers and clusters feed one network |
| User plugs into a socket | User submits a job through a portal |
| User does not know which plant supplied the power | User does not know which node ran the job |
| Pay for the electricity consumed | Use (and often account for) the resources consumed |
| Power comes on demand | Computing power comes on demand |
:::

::: {.body-text-m}
**Key idea:** computing power is treated as a **utility** that is available when needed.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Basic Idea"}

[The Basic Idea: Divide, Distribute, Combine]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    J[Large Job] --> S[Split into Small Tasks]
    S --> N1[Node 1]
    S --> N2[Node 2]
    S --> N3[Node 3]
    S --> N4[Node N]
    N1 --> C[Combine Results]
    N2 --> C
    N3 --> C
    N4 --> C
    C --> R[Final Result]
```

::: {.body-text-m}
- A large problem is **divided** into many independent sub-tasks.
- Sub-tasks run **in parallel** on different nodes.
- Partial results are **collected and combined**.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Features"}

[Key Features of Grid Computing]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Resource sharing:** processors, storage, data, and software are pooled across organisations.
- **Distributed and geographically dispersed:** nodes may be in different cities or countries.
- **Heterogeneity:** different hardware, operating systems, and networks work together.
- **Scalability:** capacity grows by adding more nodes.
- **Loose coupling:** nodes are independent and connected over standard networks.
- **Decentralised administration:** each site controls its own resources and policies.
- **Transparency:** the user sees one virtual system, not the individual machines.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="More Features"}

[More Features of a Grid]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Better utilisation:** idle computing cycles are put to productive use.
- **Reliability:** if one node fails, its task can be **rescheduled** to another node.
- **Cost effectiveness:** existing hardware is reused instead of buying a supercomputer.
- **Dynamic and on-demand:** nodes can join or leave the grid at any time.
- **Security:** authentication, authorisation, and encryption protect shared resources.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Types of Grids"}

[Types of Grids]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
| Type | Main Purpose | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Computational grid | Provide large processing power for compute-heavy tasks | Climate and weather simulation |
| Data grid | Store, manage, and share very large datasets across sites | Particle-physics experiment data |
| Collaborative grid | Let distributed teams share tools and work together | Joint research projects |
| Volunteer grid | Use donated spare cycles from personal computers | SETI@home, Folding@home |
| Enterprise grid | Share resources within one organisation | Bank or company-wide computation |
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Architecture"}

[Architecture of a Computing Grid]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    U[User / Application] --> P[Grid Portal and User Interface]
    P --> M[Grid Middleware]
    M --> RM[Resource Management and Scheduler]
    M --> SEC[Security and Authentication]
    M --> INF[Information and Monitoring Services]
    RM --> A[Node: Server]
    RM --> B[Node: Cluster]
    RM --> C[Node: Desktop PC]
    RM --> D[Node: Storage / Instrument]
```

::: {.body-text-m}
- The grid is organised as **layers**, from user applications down to the physical resources.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Grid Layers"}

[Layers of the Grid]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
| Layer | Role | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Application and portal layer | Where users submit jobs and see results | Science gateways, web portals, command-line tools |
| Middleware layer | Hides complexity; provides scheduling, security, data transfer, and monitoring | Globus Toolkit, BOINC, HTCondor |
| Resource layer | Controls access to individual resources and reports their status | Local resource managers on each site |
| Fabric layer | The actual physical resources | Servers, clusters, desktops, storage, sensors, instruments |
| Network | Connects all layers and nodes | Internet, high-speed research networks |
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Roles of Nodes"}

[Main Components and Their Roles]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Control (coordinator) node:** accepts jobs, divides them, and keeps track of progress.
- **Provider (worker) nodes:** contribute CPU, memory, and storage to run the tasks.
- **User (client) node:** submits the job and receives the result.
- **Scheduler:** decides which task runs on which node, based on load and availability.
- **Middleware:** software that glues everything together and hides heterogeneity.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="How a Grid Works"}

[How Does a Grid Work?]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[1. User submits job] --> B[2. Authenticate and authorise]
    B --> C[3. Discover available resources]
    C --> D[4. Divide job and schedule tasks]
    D --> E[5. Execute tasks on nodes]
    E --> F[6. Monitor and handle failures]
    F --> G[7. Collect and return results]
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.incremental .body-text-m}
- **Submit:** job and its requirements are sent to the grid.
- **Authenticate:** identity and permissions are checked.
- **Discover:** middleware finds nodes with suitable free resources.
- **Schedule:** tasks are mapped to nodes.
- **Execute and monitor:** failed tasks are re-run elsewhere.
- **Return:** results are merged and given to the user.
:::
:::
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Middleware"}

[Role of Grid Middleware]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
Middleware sits **between applications and the heterogeneous resources** and provides:

- **Resource discovery and allocation:** find and reserve suitable nodes.
- **Job scheduling:** queue, prioritise, and place tasks.
- **Data management:** move and replicate large files between sites.
- **Security services:** single sign-on, certificates, and access control.
- **Monitoring and fault handling:** detect failures and restart tasks.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Cluster Computing"}

[Quick Recap: Cluster Computing]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- A **cluster** is a group of similar computers, usually in **one location**, connected by a fast local network.
- All nodes are managed **centrally** by a single owner.
- The cluster works as **one tightly coupled system** for a shared task.
- Typical use: high-performance computing inside a university lab or data centre.

**Difference in one line:** a cluster is **tightly coupled and homogeneous**; a grid is **loosely coupled and heterogeneous**.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Grid vs Cluster"}

[Grid Computing vs Cluster Computing]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
| Feature | Grid Computing | Cluster Computing |
|---|---|---|
| Location | Geographically dispersed | Usually in one location |
| Hardware | Heterogeneous | Mostly homogeneous |
| Coupling | Loosely coupled | Tightly coupled |
| Ownership and control | Many organisations; decentralised | Single organisation; centralised |
| Network | Wide-area network or internet | Fast local-area network |
| Task type | Large, independent, parallel jobs | Closely cooperating parallel jobs |
| Node status | Nodes can join or leave | Fixed set of nodes |
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Grid vs Cloud"}

[Grid Computing vs Cloud Computing]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
| Feature | Grid Computing | Cloud Computing |
|---|---|---|
| Main goal | Combine resources to solve one very large problem | Provide on-demand services to many users |
| Ownership | Shared among participating organisations | Owned by a provider (AWS, Google, Microsoft, IBM) |
| Resource model | Resources pooled and shared | Resources virtualised and rented |
| Typical users | Scientists and research communities | Businesses, developers, and general users |
| Billing | Usually based on sharing agreements | Pay-as-you-go |
| Access | Through grid middleware and certificates | Through web portals and APIs |
| Scaling | Add more partner nodes | Elastic scaling on demand |
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Three-Way Comparison"}

[Grid, Cluster, and Cloud at a Glance]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
| Aspect | Cluster | Grid | Cloud |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control | Single owner | Multiple owners | Provider |
| Distance | Same site | Worldwide | Worldwide data centres |
| Coupling | Tight | Loose | Loosely coupled services |
| Best for | High-performance tasks in one place | Large collaborative science | Everyday business and applications |
| Memory aid | "One room" | "Many organisations" | "Rent a service" |
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Advantages"}

[Advantages of Grid Computing]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- Solves **very large problems** that a single machine cannot handle.
- **Reduces cost** by reusing existing, idle hardware.
- Provides **high throughput** through parallel execution.
- **Scales** easily by adding nodes.
- Gives **fault tolerance**: failed tasks can be moved to other nodes.
- Encourages **collaboration** and data sharing between institutions.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Limitations"}

[Limitations and Challenges]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Security and trust:** data and code run on machines owned by others.
- **Complex setup:** installing, configuring, and maintaining middleware needs expertise.
- **Heterogeneity:** different systems make compatibility and standardisation difficult.
- **Network dependence:** slow or unreliable links delay tasks and data transfer.
- **Not suited to every job:** tightly coupled tasks that need constant communication run poorly.
- **Unpredictable availability:** nodes may leave mid-task, especially in volunteer grids.
- **Scheduling and policy issues:** fair sharing among organisations is hard to manage.
- **Administrative and legal barriers:** differing policies, data-protection rules, and ownership.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Applications"}

[Application Areas of Grid Computing]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
| Area | Use of Grid Computing |
|---|---|
| Scientific research | Particle physics, astronomy, and climate modelling |
| Healthcare and life sciences | Genome analysis, protein folding, drug discovery |
| Engineering | Aircraft and automobile design simulations, crash testing |
| Finance | Risk analysis, portfolio simulation, fraud detection |
| Weather and earth sciences | Weather forecasting, earthquake and flood modelling |
| Entertainment | Rendering animation and visual effects |
| Education and e-science | Sharing data, tools, and instruments among universities |
| Big data and analytics | Processing very large datasets in parallel |
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Real Examples"}

[Well-Known Grid Projects]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Worldwide LHC Computing Grid (WLCG):** shares and analyses data from CERN's Large Hadron Collider across hundreds of computing centres.
- **SETI@home:** volunteers donated idle PC time to analyse radio-telescope signals.
- **Folding@home:** volunteer computers simulate protein folding to support disease research.
- **BOINC:** an open platform used by many volunteer-computing science projects.
- **National research grids:** academic networks that link supercomputing and data resources, such as India's research-computing initiatives.
:::

---

## {data-menu-title="Case Study"}

[Case Study: Analysing Particle-Physics Data]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- **Problem:** a large physics experiment produces **petabytes of data every year**, far beyond any one institution.
- **Grid solution:** data is stored and replicated across **many computing centres worldwide**, and analysis jobs are sent to where the data and free processors are.
- **Benefit:** thousands of researchers in different countries analyse the same data at once, using shared resources.
- **Challenge:** moving huge datasets, keeping data secure, and coordinating many organisations.

**Lesson:** the grid turns separate institutional resources into one shared scientific infrastructure.
:::

## {data-menu-title="Activity"}

[Quick Activity (3 minutes)]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
Decide whether each situation suits **cluster**, **grid**, or **cloud**, and justify your choice:

1. A university lab runs a weather simulation on 32 identical servers in one room.
2. Universities in five countries pool computers to process a shared genome dataset.
3. A start-up rents servers by the hour to host its mobile-app backend.
4. Volunteers donate idle PC time to search for signals from space.
:::

## {data-menu-title="Key Concepts"}

[Important Definitions and Key Terminology]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
- **Grid computing:** a network of dispersed, heterogeneous resources working together as one virtual supercomputer.
- **Node:** an individual computer or resource in the grid.
- **Middleware:** software layer that manages resources, scheduling, and security.
- **Scheduler:** component that assigns tasks to suitable nodes.
- **Virtual organisation:** a group of people and institutions sharing grid resources under agreed rules.
- **Heterogeneous:** made up of different types of hardware and software.
- **Loosely coupled:** nodes are independent and communicate over a network.
- **Volunteer computing:** donating idle computer time to a project.
- **Utility computing:** providing computing power on demand like electricity.
:::

## {data-menu-title="Summary"}

[Lecture Summary]{.slide-title}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-m}
- Grid computing links dispersed, heterogeneous computers into one virtual supercomputer.
- Its key features are resource sharing, scalability, heterogeneity, loose coupling, and decentralised control.
- A grid has application, middleware, resource, and fabric layers; middleware handles scheduling, security, and monitoring.
- A cluster is tightly coupled and local, a grid is loosely coupled and multi-organisational, and a cloud offers on-demand rented services.
- Major challenges are security, complex setup, network dependence, and unpredictable node availability.
- Grids are widely used in science, healthcare, engineering, finance, and weather forecasting.
:::

## {data-menu-title="Knowledge Check"}

[Knowledge Check: MCQs]{.slide-title2}

<hr>

::: {.body-text-s}
1. Grid computing mainly combines:  
   A. Only identical computers in one room  B. Dispersed and heterogeneous resources  C. Only printers  D. Only mobile phones  
   **Answer: B**

2. Software that manages scheduling, security, and resource discovery in a grid is called:  
   A. Middleware  B. Firmware  C. Spreadsheet  D. Compiler  
   **Answer: A**

3. Which statement about a cluster is correct?  
   A. Loosely coupled and worldwide  B. Usually tightly coupled and in one location  C. Always volunteer-based  D. Needs no network  
   **Answer: B**

4. SETI@home is an example of:  
   A. Volunteer grid computing  B. Augmented reality  C. Blockchain mining only  D. A word processor  
   **Answer: A**

5. A major limitation of grid computing is:  
   A. It cannot use parallel processing  B. Security and trust across organisations  C. It works only with one computer  D. It has no applications  
   **Answer: B**
:::
